The solver’s container now holds only the base commit, with no test history and no copy of the benchmark repository, and grading runs in a separate evaluator container; the missing interfaces are stated in the stubs or instructions the agent can see, without copying any test cases; the editor files are included in the solver’s workspace; and the evaluator strips the @Disabled annotations before running the Java tests. All 225 reference solutions pass under our repaired setup, so every task remains solvable. We then re-evaluated the two agents DGM reported: the initial agent and the final “best” agent produced by its evolution run. Since the o3-mini model DGM originally used is no longer available, both agents use gpt-5.4-mini as the solver backbone. Due to a limited budget we did not re-run the entire evolution itself. Instead, we ask whether its final evolved agent is better than its initial one in our repaired Polyglot environment. To see how much the environment correction alone moves the scores, we also ran both agents in DGM’s flawed setup.

On our repaired benchmark, the initial agent solves 91 of 225 tasks (40.4%) and the evolved agent solves 88 (39.1%). The two agents solve a largely overlapping set: 69 tasks are solved by both, 22 only by the initial agent, and 19 only by the evolved one.

  Original environment (flawed) Repaired environment
Initial agent 28.4% 40.4%
Best agent from DGM evolution 29.8% 39.1%
Success rate on all 225 Polyglot tasks with gpt-5.4-mini as the solver.

As a sanity check on our recreation of the original environment: DGM’s own transfer experiment, which swaps o3-mini for Sonnet 3.5 or 3.7, reports the best agent ahead of the initial one by 1.3 and 1.2 percentage points. We measure 1.4 with gpt-5.4-mini.

The table is not a test of DGM’s evolution procedure, since the best agent was selected with o3-mini in the original environment. We therefore do not try to conclude whether DGM’s reported gain, from 14.2% to 30.7%, was produced by the flawed environment. What the table does show is how unreliable the original environment is as a parent-selection signal. Holding the agent fixed, repairing the environment moves the score by up to 12 points (28.4% vs 40.4%). The initial and evolved agents, by contrast, differ by only about one point in either environment. A sound evaluation environment is a precondition for meaningful self-improvement. In a flawed environment, evolution can favor policies that exploit those flaws over policies that improve coding ability.

Reflections

Our intention is not to discredit the contribution of DGM and its successors in the field of recursive self-improving agents. We appreciate DGM’s work and the authors’ openness in sharing their implementation and detailed evolution traces with the research community; this post was only possible because of it.

The recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident showed that LLM agents can exploit their environment to cheat on their tasks. In the incident, agents that had unintentionally been given impossible tasks went looking for a way around the scorer, and the sandboxes meant to isolate them did not hold. We saw the same pattern play out on a much smaller scale in Polyglot: tasks that could not be solved as given (due to missing contracts or files), and a stronger solver that went looking for the hidden tests and used them. The prompt was the only defense, and it failed.

When building environments and sandboxes for self-evolving systems, we believe two things are needed. First, the benchmark’s original testing protocol must be fully understood before it is adapted, so that the agent is given a fair task. Second, access boundaries should be enforced by the sandbox rather than entrusted to the prompt. As agents become more capable, guardrails that held for weaker agents may no longer be effective, and we consider the study of how and when that happens an important direction for future work.
entry.summary: Self-evolving coding agents such as Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) use their scores on a coding benchmark to guide changes to their own harnesses, such as their tools and workflows. We find four flaws in DGM’s adaptation of Aider’s Polyglot benchmark that make these scores an unreliable signal of which harness changes improve a coding agent. Later systems such as Huxley-Gödel Machine reuse the same evaluation setup and inherit these flaws. In this misconfigured Polyglot environment, agents can access hidden tests and solutions, task contracts and supporting files are missing, and most Java tests are skipped. Repairing the environment shifts the score of the same gpt-5.4-mini agent by up to 12 percentage points. This sensitivity to the evaluation setup warrants revisiting DGM’s reported gains on Polyglot, and it shows that a correct environment is a precondition for reliable self-evolving systems.

entry.title: Getting SAC to Work on a Massively Parallel Simulator: An RL Journey With Off-Policy Algorithms

link.title: Getting SAC to Work on a Massively Parallel Simulator: An RL Journey With Off-Policy Algorithms

entry.content:
Spoiler alert: quite a few papers/code are affected by the problem described below.

This post is divided into two main parts. The first part analyzes why SAC does not work out of the box in Isaac Sim environments (until the quick fix section). The second part discusses how to tune SAC for speed and make it perform as good as PPO.

A Suspicious Trend: PPO, PPO, PPO, …

The story begins a while ago when I saw another paper using the same recipe for learning locomotion: train a PPO agent in simulation using thousands of environments in parallel and domain randomization, then deploy it on the real robot. This recipe has become the standard since 2021, when ETH Zurich and NVIDIA showed that it was possible to learn locomotion in minutes on a single workstation. The codebase and the simulator (called Isaac Gym at that time) that were published became the basis for much follow-up workLike the BD-1 Disney robot.

As an RL researcher interested in learning directly on real robots, I was curious and suspicious about one aspect of this trend: why is no one trying an algorithm other than PPOI was not the only one asking why SAC doesn't work: nvidia forum reddit1 reddit2? PPO benefits from fast and parallel environments, but PPO is not the only deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithm for continuous control tasks, and there are alternatives like SAC or TQC that can lead to better performance.

So I decided to investigate why practitioners do not use these off-policy algorithms, and maybe why they don’t work with massively parallel simulatorsSince the first version of this post was written over a year ago, I'm glad to see follow-up work such as FastTD3, FlashSAC or others that investigate this further..

Why It Matters? - Fine Tuning on Real Robots

If we could make SAC work with these simulators, then it would be possible to train in simulation and fine-tune on the real robot using the same algorithm (PPO is too sample-inefficient to train on a single robot).

By using other algorithms, it might also be possible to get better performance. Finally, it is always good to better understand what works or not and why. As researchers, we tend to publish only positive results, but a lot of valuable insights are lost in our unpublished failures.

(The Path of Least Resistance) Hypothesis

Before digging any further, I had some hypotheses as to why PPO was the only algorithm used:

  • PPO is fast to train (in terms of computation time) and was tuned for the massively parallel environment.
  • As researchers, we tend to take the path of least resistance and build on proven solutions (the original training code is open source, and the simulator is freely available) to get new, interesting resultsYes, we tend to be lazy..
  • Some peculiarities in the environment design may favor PPO over other algorithms. In other words, the massively parallel environments might be optimized for PPO.
  • SAC/TQC and derivatives are tuned for sample efficiency, not fast wall clock time. In the case of massively parallel simulation, what matters is how long it takes to train, not how many samples are used. They probably need to be tuned/adjusted for this new setting.

Note: During my journey, I will be using Stable-Baselines3 and its fast Jax version SBX.

The Hunt Begins

There are now many massively parallel simulators available (Isaac Sim, Brax, MJX, Genesis, Newton, …). Here, I will focus on locomotion tasks in Isaac Sim: locomotion was one of the first and most successful applications of massively parallel simulation, and Isaac Sim was one of the earliest and most influential simulators.

A PPO agent trained on the Isaac-Velocity-Flat-Unitree-A1-v0 locomotion task.
Green arrow is the desired velocity, blue arrow represents the current velocity

As with any RL problem, starting simple is the key to success Also known as Gall's law. Therefore, I decided to focus on the Isaac-Velocity-Flat-Unitree-A1-v0 locomotion task first, because it is simple but representative. The goal is to learn a policy that can move the Unitree A1 quadruped in any direction on flat ground, following a commanded velocity (the same way you would control a robot with a joystick). The agent receives information about its current task as input (joint positions, velocities, desired velocity, …) and outputs desired joint positions (12D vector, three joints per leg). The robot is rewarded for following the correct desired velocity (linear and angular) and for other secondary tasks (feet air time, smooth control, …). An episode ends when the robot falls over or times out after 1000 stepsThe control loop runs at 50 Hz, so after 20 seconds.

To begin, I did some sanity checks. I ran PPO with the tuned hyperparameters found in the repository, and it was able to quickly solve the task. In 5 minutes, it gets an average episode return of ~30 (above an episode return of 15, the task is almost solved). Then I tried SAC and TQC, with default hyperparameters (and observation normalization), and, as expected, it didn’t work. No matter how long it was training, there was no sign of improvement.

Looking at the simulation GUI, something struck me: the robots were making very large random movements. Something was wrong.

SAC out of the box on Isaac Sim during training.

Because of the very large movements, I suspected the problem had to do with the actions the robot was allowed to take. Looking at the code, the RL agent commands a (scaled) delta with respect to a default joint position:

# Note desired_joint_pos is of dimension 12 (3 joints per leg)
desired_joint_pos = default_joint_pos + scale * action

Then, let’s look at the action space itself (I’m using ipdb to have an interactive debugger):

import ipdb; ipdb.set_trace()
>> vec_env.action_space
Box(-100.0, 100.0, (12,), float32)

Ah ah! The action space defines continuous actions of dimension 12 (nothing wrong here), but the limits \([-100, 100]\) are surprisingly large, e.g., it allows a delta of +/- 1432 degrees!! in joint angle when scale=0.25, like for the Unitree A1 robot. To understand why normalizing the action space matters (usually a bounded space in \([-1, 1]\)), we need to dig deeper into how PPO works.

Note: those bounds are defined by the IsaacLab SB3 wrapper; the actual original action space is defined as Box(-inf, inf, (12,), float32), fully unbounded!

PPO Gaussian Distribution

Like many RL algorithms, PPO relies on a probability distribution to select actions. During training, at each timestep, it samples an action \(a_t \sim N(\mu_\theta(s_t), \sigma^2)\) from a Gaussian distribution in the case of continuous actionsThis is not true for the PPO implementation in Brax which uses a squashed Gaussian like SAC.. The mean of the Gaussian \(\mu_\theta(s_t)\) is the output of the actor neural network (with parameters \(\theta\)) and the standard deviation is a learnable parameter \(\sigma\), usually initialized with \(\sigma_0 = 1.0\).

This means that at the beginning of training, most of the sampled actions will be in \([-3, 3]\) (from the Three Sigma Rule):

The initial Gaussian distribution used by PPO for sampling actions.

Back to our original topic, because of the way \(\sigma\) is initialized, if the action space has large bounds (upper/lower bounds » 1), PPO will almost never sample actions near the limits. In practice, the actions taken by PPO will be far from them. Now, let’s compare the initial PPO action distribution with the Unitree A1 action space:

The same initial Gaussian distribution, but with the perspective of the Unitree A1 action space $$[-100, 100]$$

For reference, we can plot the action distribution of PPO after trainingThe code to record and plot action distribution is in the Appendix:

Distribution of actions for PPO after training (on 64 000 steps).

The min/max values per dimension:

>> actions.min(axis=0)
array([-3.6, -2.5, -3.1, -1.8, -4.5, -4.2, -4. , -3.9, -2.8, -2.8, -2.9, -2.7])
>> actions.max(axis=0)
array([ 3.2,  2.8,  2.7,  2.8,  2.9,  2.7,  3.2,  2.9,  7.2,  5.7,  5. ,  5.8])

Again, most of the actions are centered around zero (which makes sense, since it corresponds to the quadruped initial position, which is usually chosen to be stable), and there are almost no actions outside \([-5, 5]\) (less than 0.1%): PPO uses less than 5% of the action space!

Now that we know that we need less than 5% of the action space to solve the task, let’s see why this might explain why SAC doesn’t work in this caseAction spaces that are too small are also problematic. See SB3 RL Tips and Tricks..

SAC Squashed Gaussian

SAC and other off-policy algorithms for continuous actions (such as DDPG, TD3, or TQC) have an additional transformation at the end of the actor network. In SAC, actions are sampled from an unbounded Gaussian distribution and then passed through a \(tanh()\) function to squash them to the range \([-1, 1]\). SAC then linearly rescales the sampled action to match the action space definition, i.e. it transforms the action from \([-1, 1]\) to \([\text{low}, \text{high}]\)Rescale from [-1, 1] to [low, high] using action = low + (0.5 * (scaled_action + 1.0) * (high - low))..

What does this mean? Assuming we start with a standard deviation similar to PPO, this is what the sampled action distribution looks like after squashingCommon PPO implementations clip the actions to fit the desired boundaries, which has the effect of oversampling actions at the boundaries when the limits are smaller than ~4.:

The equivalent initial squashed Gaussian distribution.

And after rescaling to the environment limits (with PPO distribution to put it in perspective):

The same initial squashed Gaussian distribution but rescaled to the Unitree A1 action space $$[-100, 100]$$

As you can see, these are two completely different initial distributions at the beginning of training! The fact that the actions are rescaled to fit the action space boundaries explains the very large movements seen during training. Also, it explains why it was impossible for SAC to learn anything useful.

Quick Fix

When I discovered that the action limits were way too large, my first reflex was to re-train SAC, but with only 3% of the action space, to more or less match the effective action space of PPO. Although it didn’t reach PPO performance, there was finally some sign of life (an average episodic return slightly positive after a while).

Next, looking at the entropy coefficient dynamics, I reduced SAC exploration by having a smaller entropy coefficientThe entropy coeff is the coeff that does the trade-off between RL objective and entropy maximization. at the beginning of trainingI also used a neural network similar to the one used by PPO to improve performance, see ablation study in appendix.. Bingo! SAC finally learned to solve the task!

Learning curve on the Unitree A1 task using 1024 envs.
Trained SAC agent after the quick fix.

SAC Hyperparameters (the ones not specified are SB3/SBX defaults):

sac_hyperparams = dict(
    policy_kwargs={
        # Similar to PPO network tuned for Unitree A1 task
        "activation_fn": jax.nn.elu,
        "net_arch": [512, 256, 128],
    },
    # Reduce the update-to-data ratio for faster training
    gradient_steps=32,
    # Reduce initial exploration/entropy coefficient
    ent_coef="auto_0.006",
)

If you are curious about the details (entropy coefficient plot, impact of the larger neural network, …), you can find an ablation study in the appendix.

Transition: What Does That Mean for the RL Community?

When I discovered the large action limits problem, I was curious to see how widespread it was in the community. After a quick search, it turns out that a lot of papers/code are affectedA notable exception are Brax-based environments because their PPO implementation uses a squashed Gaussian, so the boundaries of the environments had to be properly defined. by this large boundary problem (see a non-exhaustive list of affected papers/code below).

Although the initial choice of bounds may be a conscious and convenient one (no need to specify the real bounds, PPO will figure it out), it seems to have worked a bit by accident for those who built on top of it, and probably discouraged practitioners from trying other algorithms.

My recommendation would be to always have properly defined action bounds. If they are not known in advance, you can plot the action distribution and adjust the limits when iterating on the environment design More on that very soon ;).

Tuning for Speed (Part II)

Although SAC can now solve the locomotion task on flat ground, it takes more time to train, is not consistent, and the performance is slightly below PPO’s. In addition, SAC’s learned gaits are not as pleasing as PPO’s, for example, SAC agents tend to keep one leg up in the air…

The second part of this post explores these aspectsI also present the ideas that didn't work and could use help (open problems) at the end of this post., as well as more complex environments. It also details how to automatically tune SAC for speed (i.e., minimize wall clock time), to learn as fast as PPO.

Although the technique I present here to make SAC work is tailored to a specific setting, the reasoning and approach should be applicable beyond this blog post. This is in line with AutoRL’s goal of making RL work out of the box in arbitrary contexts.

Defining Proper Action Bound - Extracting the Limits with PPO

First, let’s define the action space more precisely. Correctly defining the boundaries of the action space is important for both the convergence speed and the final performance. A larger action space gives the agent more flexibility, which can lead to better performance, but slower learning. Conversely, a smaller action space can accelerate learning, though it may result in suboptimal solutions.

Thus, rather than simply restricting the action space to a small percentage of the original, I recorded the actions taken by a trained PPO agent and took the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles for the new limits. In other words, the new action space contains 95% of the actions commanded by a trained PPO agentI repeat the same process for any new environment where those boundaries would not work:

# np.percentile(actions, 2.5, axis=0)
low = np.array([-2.0, -0.4, -2.6, -1.3, -2.2, -1.9, -0.7, -0.4, -2.1, -2.4, -2.5, -1.7])
# np.percentile(actions, 97.5, axis=0)
high = np.array([1.1, 2.6, 0.7, 1.9, 1.3, 2.6, 3.4, 3.8, 3.4, 3.4, 1.9, 2.1])

It is not a requirement to use a trained PPO agent to define the limits. In the “quick fix” section, a simple rescaling (3% of the original space) was already enough. The percentiles make the choice more principled and less arbitrary. Ideally, these action limits would be properly defined directly in the base environment.

Need for Speed or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying About Sample Efficiency

The second aspect I can improve is the hyperparameters of the SAC algorithm. The default hyperparameters of the SAC algorithm are optimized for sample efficiency. While this is ideal for learning directly on a single real robot, it is suboptimal for training thousands of robots in simulation.

Previously, I quickly tuned SAC by hand to get it up and running. This was sufficient for obtaining initial results, but it would be very time-consuming to continue tuning manually to reach PPO’s performance level. That’s why I turned to automatic hyperparameter optimization.

New Objective: Learn as Fast as Possible

Since I’m using a massively parallel simulator, I no longer care about how many samples are needed to learn something but how quickly it can learn, regardless of the number of samples used. In practice, this translates to an objective function that looks like this:

def objective(trial: optuna.Trial) -> float:
    """Optimize for best performance after 5 minutes of training."""
    # Sample hyperparameters
    hyperparams = sample_sac_params(trial)
    agent = sbx.SAC(env=env, **hyperparams)
    # Callback to exit the training loop after 5 minutes
    callback = TimeoutCallback(timeout=60 * 5)
    # Train with a max budget of 50_000_000 timesteps
    agent.learn(total_timesteps=int(5e7), callback=callback)
    # Log the number of interactions with the environments
    trial.set_user_attr("num_timesteps", agent.num_timesteps)
    # Evaluate the trained agent
    env.seed(args_cli.seed)
    mean_reward, std_reward = evaluate_policy(agent, env, n_eval_episodes=512)
    return mean_reward

The agent is evaluated after five minutes of training, regardless of how many interactions with the environment were needed (the TimeoutCallback forces the agent to exit the training loop).

SAC Hyperparameters Sampler

Similar to PPO, many hyperparameters can be tuned for SAC. After some trial and error, I came up with the following sampling function (I’ve included comments that explain the meaning of each parameter):

def sample_sac_params(trial: optuna.Trial) -> dict[str, Any]:
    # Discount factor
    gamma = trial.suggest_float("gamma", 0.975, 0.995)
    learning_rate = trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 1e-4, 0.002, log=True)
    # Initial exploration rate (entropy coefficient in the SAC loss)
    ent_coef_init = trial.suggest_float("ent_coef_init", 0.001, 0.02, log=True)
    # From 2^7=128 to 2^12 = 4096, the mini-batch size
    batch_size_pow = trial.suggest_int("batch_size_pow", 7, 12, log=True)
    # How big should the actor and critic networks be
    # net_arch = trial.suggest_categorical("net_arch", ["default", "simba", "large"])
    # I'm using integers to be able to use CMA-ES,
    # "default" is [256, 256], "large" is [512, 256, 128]
    net_arch_complexity = trial.suggest_int("net_arch_complexity", 0, 3)
    # From 1 to 8 (how often should we update the networks, every train_freq steps in the env)
    train_freq_pow = trial.suggest_int("train_freq_pow", 0, 3)
    # From 1 to 1024 (how many gradient steps by step in the environment)
    gradient_steps_pow = trial.suggest_int("gradient_steps_pow", 0, 10)
    # From 1 to 32 (the policy delay parameter, similar to TD3 update)
    policy_delay_pow = trial.suggest_int("policy_delay_pow", 0, 5)
    # Polyak coeff (soft update of the target network)
    tau = trial.suggest_float("tau", 0.001, 0.05, log=True)

    # Display true values
    trial.set_user_attr("batch_size", 2**batch_size_pow)
    trial.set_user_attr("gradient_steps", 2**gradient_steps_pow)
    trial.set_user_attr("policy_delay", 2**policy_delay_pow)
    trial.set_user_attr("train_freq", 2**train_freq_pow)
    # Note: to_hyperparams() does the conversions between sampled value and expected value
    # Ex: converts batch_size_pow to batch_size
    # This is useful when replaying trials
    return to_hyperparams({
        "train_freq_pow": train_freq_pow,
        "gradient_steps_pow": gradient_steps_pow,
        "batch_size_pow": batch_size_pow,
        "tau": tau,
        "gamma": gamma,
        "learning_rate": learning_rate,
        "policy_delay_pow": policy_delay_pow,
        "ent_coef_init": ent_coef_init,
        "net_arch_complexity": net_arch_complexity,
    })

Replay Ratio

A metric that will be useful to understand the tuned hyperparameters is the replay ratio. The replay ratio (also known as update-to-data ratio or UTD ratio) measures the number of gradient updates performed per environment interaction or experience collected. This ratio represents how often an agent updates its parameters relative to how much new experience it gathers. For SAC, it is defined as replay_ratio = gradient_steps / (num_envs * train_freq).

In a classic setting, the replay ratio is usually greater than one when optimizing for sample efficiency. That means that SAC does at least one gradient step per interaction with the environment. However, since collecting new data is cheap in the current setting, the replay ratio tends to be lower than 1/10 (one gradient step for every ten steps in the environment).

Optimization Result - Tuned Hyperparameters

To optimize the hyperparameters, I used Optuna’s CMA-ES sampler for 100 trialsHere, I only optimized for the Unitree A1 flat task due to limited computation power. It would be interesting to tune SAC directly for the "Rough" variant, including `n_steps` and gSDE train frequency as hyperparameters. (taking about 10 hours with a population size of 10 individuals). Afterward, I retrained the best trials to filter out any lucky seeds, i.e., to find hyperparameters that work consistently across different runs.

This is what the optimization history looks like. Many sets of hyperparameters were successful:

Hyperparameter optimization history

These are the tuned hyperparameters of SAC found by the CMA-ES sampler while optimizing for speed:

batch_size: 512
buffer_size: 2_000_000
ent_coef: auto_0.009471776840423638
gamma: 0.983100250213744
gradient_steps: 32
learning_rate: 0.00044689099625712413
learning_starts: 2000
policy: MlpPolicy
policy_delay: 8
policy_kwargs:
  net_arch: [512, 256, 128]
  activation_fn: !!python/name:isaaclab_rl.sb3.elu ''
  optimizer_class: !!python/name:optax._src.alias.adamw ''
  layer_norm: true
tau: 0.0023055560568780655
train_freq: 1

Compared to the default hyperparameters of SAC, there are some notable changes:

  • The network architecture is much larger ([512, 256, 128] vs. [256, 256]), but similar to that used by PPO in Isaac Sim.
  • The lower replay ratio (RR ≈ 0.03 for 1024 environments, or three gradient steps every 100 steps in an environment) and higher policy delay (update the actor once every eight critic updates) make it faster, as less time is taken for gradient updates.
  • The discount factor is lower than the default value of 0.99, which favors shorter-term rewards.

Here is the result in video and the associated learning curves:

Learning curve on the Unitree A1 task using 1024 envs. The 95% confidence interval is computed using bootstrapping.
Trained SAC agent after automatic tuning.

With these tuned hyperparameters, SAC learns faster than before, achieves higher performance, and the learned gaits look better (no more feet in the air!). What more could you ask for?

Does it work? - More Environments

After it successfully learned in the flat Unitree A1 environment, I tested the same hyperparameters (with the same recipeI updated the limits for each family of robots. The PPO percentiles technique worked nicely.) on the GO1, GO2, Anymal-B, and Anymal-C environments, as well as the flat Disney BD-X environment, and … it worked!

Trained SAC agent in different environments, using the same tuned hyperparameters.

Then, I trained SAC on the “rough” locomotion environments, which are harder environments where the robot has to learn to navigate steps and uneven, rough terrain (with additional randomization). And … it worked partially.

Solving Harder Environments

Identifying the problem: Why it doesn’t work?

In the “Rough” environment, the SAC-trained agent exhibits inconsistent behavior. For example, one time the robot successfully climbs down the pyramid steps without falling; at other times, however, it does nothing. Additionally, no matter how long it is trained, SAC does not seem to be able to learn to solve the “inverted pyramid”, which is probably one of the most challenging tasks:

The inverted pyramid task.

I isolated this task by training SAC only on the inverted pyramid. Upon further inspection, it appeared to be an exploration problem; that is, SAC never experiences successful stepping when executing random movements. This reminded me of SAC failing on the mountain car problem because the exploration was inconsistent (the default high-frequency noise is usually a bad default for robots).

Improving Exploration and Performance

To test this hypothesis, I simplified the problem by reducing the height of the inverted-pyramid steps. I also used a more consistent exploration scheme: generalized State-Dependent Exploration (gSDE).

In its simplest form, gSDE repeats the noise vector for \(n\)-steps, instead of sampling it at every timestep. In other words, instead of selecting actions following \(a_t = \mu_\theta(s_t) + \epsilon_t\)$$\mu_\theta(s_t)$$ is the actor network output, which represents the mean of the Gaussian distribution. and sampling \(\epsilon_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) at every step during exploration, gSDE samples \(\epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) once and keeps \(\epsilon\) constant for \(n\)-steps. The robot could finally learn to partially solve this task with this improved exploration.

Trained SAC agent with gSDE and n-step return in the "Rough" Anymal-C environment.

There was still a big gap in final performance between SAC and PPO. To close the gap, I drew inspiration from the recent FastTD3 paper and implemented n-step returns. Using n_steps=3 allowed SAC to finally solve the hardest task!

In summary, here are the additional manual changes I made to the hyperparameters of SAC compared to those optimized automatically:

# Note: we must use train_freq > 1 to enable gSDE
# which resamples the noise every n steps (here every 10 steps)
train_freq: 10
# Scaling the gradient steps accordingly, to keep the same replay ratio:
# 32 * train_freq = 320
gradient_steps: 320
use_sde: True
# N-step return
n_steps: 3

And here are the associated learning curves (plotting the current curriculum level on the y-axisI'm plotting the current state of the terrain curriculum (the higher the number, the harder the task/terrain) as the reward magnitude doesn't tell the whole story for the "Rough" task.):

Learning curve on the Anymal-C "Rough" task using 1024 envs and 10 seeds. The 95% confidence interval is computed using bootstrapping.
Learning curve in terms of sample-efficiency on the Anymal-C "Rough" task using 1024 envs and 10 seeds.

In those plots, you can see the effect of gSDE and the use of n-step returns. SAC is also much more sample-efficient than PPO.

Conclusion

This concludes the long journey I started a while ago to make SAC work on a massively parallel simulator. During this adventure, I addressed a common issue that prevents SAC-like algorithms from working in these environments: the use of an unbounded action space.

In the end, with a proper action space and tuned hyperparameters, SAC is now competitive with PPO in terms of training time (while being much more sample-efficient) on a large collection of locomotion environments. I hope my voyage helps others solve new tasks with RL, encourages them to use SAC in their experiments, and helps unlock fine-tuning on real robots after pretraining in simulation.

Appendix: Affected Papers/Code

Please find here a non-exhaustive list of papers/code affected by the large bound problem:

  • IsaacLab
  • Learning to Walk in Minutes
  • One Policy to Run Them All
  • Genesis env
  • ASAP Humanoid
  • Agile But Robust
  • Rapid Locomotion
  • Deep Whole Body Control
  • Robot Parkour Learning

You can probably find many more by looking at works that cite the ETH paper.

  • Seems to be fixed in Extreme Parkour (clip action 1.2)
  • Almost fixed in Walk these ways (clip action 10)

Appendix: Note on Unbounded Action Spaces

While discussing this blog post with a fellow researcher, they raised another point that could explain why people might choose an unbounded action space.

In short, policies can learn to produce actions outside the joint limits to trick the underlying PD controller into outputting desired torques. For example, when recovering from a strong push, what matters is not to accurately track a desired position, but to quickly move the joints in the right direction. This makes training almost invariant to the chosen PD gains.

Appendix: Ablation Study of the Quick Fix

Ablation study of the "quick fix" on the Unitree A1 task using 10 seeds. The 95% confidence interval is computed using bootstrapping.

The main point of the “quick fix” was to have a first sign of life. However, to isolate the effects of the different modifications, I did an ablation study (see above plot).

In summary:

  • Without proper action bounds (w/ limits runs in the plot), SAC doesn’t learn anything (flat learning curve, see “baseline, original action space” plot).
  • The entropy coefficient initialization (w/ ent coef runs) is not essential to see some sign of life (learning a controller better than a random agent) but greatly improves the performance.
  • A larger network is not essential (w/ bigger net runs), but it does help to improve performance.

To understand the entropy coefficient dynamics, you can find the plots of the entropy coefficient and the associated loss below.

In short, with the default entropy coefficient initialization (ent_coef_init=1), the entropy coefficient decreases until it reaches a low enough value. If you look at the associated learning curve, this corresponds to the moment when SAC actually starts learning (episodic return steadily increasing from -10 to positive values). With a tuned ent_coef_init, SAC starts learning immediately.

Evolution of the entropy coefficient for different configurations on the Unitree A1 task.
Evolution of the entropy coefficient loss for different configurations on the Unitree A1 task.

Appendix: Setup Details

Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3070

Simulator: The main results were done using v2.0.0 (IsaacSim 4.5) and reproduced on IsaacLab v2.3.2 (IsaacSim 5.1).

The code to reproduce the results (training and hyperparameter optimization) is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/IsaacLab-697E (fork of IsaacLab).

Appendix: What I Tried That Didn’t Work

While preparing this blog post, I tried many things to achieve PPO performance and learn good policies in minimal time. Many of the things I tried didn’t work, but they are probably worth investigating further. I hope you can learn from my failures, too.

Using an Unbounded Gaussian Distribution

One approach I tried was to make SAC look more like PPO. In part one, PPO could handle an unbounded action space because it used a (non-squashed) Gaussian distribution (vs. a squashed one for SAC). However, replacing SAC’s squashed Normal distribution with an unbounded Gaussian distribution led to additional problems.

Without layer normalization in the critic, it quickly diverges (leading to Inf/NaN). It seems that, encouraged by the entropy bonus, the actor pushes toward very large action values. It also appears that this variant requires specific tuning (and that state-dependent std may need to be replaced with state-independent std, as is done for PPO).

If you manage to reliably make SAC work with an unbounded Gaussian distribution, please reach out!

KL Divergence Adaptive Learning Rate

One component of PPO that allows for better performance is the learning rate schedule (although it is not critical, it eases hyperparameter tuning). It automatically adjusts the learning rate to maintain a constant KL divergence between two updates, ensuring that the new policy remains close to the previous one (and ensuring that the learning rate is large enough, too). It should be possible to do something similar with SAC. However, when I tried to approximate the KL divergence using either the log probability or the extracted Gaussian parameters (mean and standard deviation), it didn’t work. The KL divergence values were too large and inconsistent. SAC would probably need a trust region mechanism as well.

Again, if you find a way to make it work, please reach out!

En Vrac - Other Things I Tried

  • penalty to be away from action bounds (hard to tune)
  • action space schedule (start with a small action space, make it bigger over time, tricky to schedule, and didn’t improve performance)
  • linear schedule (learning_rate = LinearSchedule(start=5e-4, end=1e-5, end_fraction=0.15)), it helped for convergence when using n_steps=1 and use_sde=False, but was not needed at the end

Appendix: Plot Action Distribution

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns
from gymnasium import spaces
from stable_baselines3 import PPO
from stable_baselines3.common.env_util import make_vec_env
from stable_baselines3.common.vec_env import VecEnvWrapper

sns.set_theme()


class PlotActionVecEnvWrapper(VecEnvWrapper):
    """
    VecEnv wrapper for plotting the taken actions.
    """

    def __init__(self, venv, plot_freq: int = 10_000):
        super().__init__(venv)
        # Action buffer
        assert isinstance(self.action_space, spaces.Box)
        self.n_actions = self.action_space.shape[0]
        self.actions = np.zeros((plot_freq, self.num_envs, self.n_actions))
        self.n_steps = 0
        self.plot_freq = plot_freq

    def reset(self):
        return self.venv.reset()

    def step_wait(self):
        obs, rewards, dones, infos = self.venv.step_wait()
        return obs, rewards, dones, infos

    def step_async(self, actions):
        self.actions[self.n_steps % self.plot_freq] = actions
        self.n_steps += 1
        if self.n_steps % self.plot_freq == 0:
            self.plot()
        self.venv.step_async(actions)

    def plot(self) -> None:
        # Flatten the env dimension
        actions = self.actions.reshape(-1, self.n_actions)
        n_steps = self.num_envs * self.n_steps
        # Create a figure with subplots for each action dimension
        n_rows = min(2, self.n_actions // 2 + 1)
        n_cols = max(self.n_actions // 2, 1)
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(12, 10))
        fig.suptitle(
            f"Distribution of Actions per Dimension after {n_steps} steps", fontsize=16
        )

        # Flatten the axes array for easy iteration
        if n_rows > 1:
            axes = axes.flatten()
        else:
            # Special case, n_actions == 1
            axes = [axes]

        # Plot the distribution for each action dimension
        for i in range(self.n_actions):
            sns.histplot(actions[:, i], kde=True, ax=axes[i], stat="density")
            axes[i].set_title(f"Action Dimension {i+1}")
            axes[i].set_xlabel("Action Value")
            axes[i].set_ylabel("Density")

        # Adjust the layout and display the plot
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()


vec_env = make_vec_env("Pendulum-v1", n_envs=2)
wrapped_env = PlotActionVecEnvWrapper(vec_env, plot_freq=5_000)

# from sbx import PPO
# from sbx import SAC
# policy_kwargs = dict(log_std_init=-0.5)

model = PPO("MlpPolicy", wrapped_env, gamma=0.98, verbose=1)
model.learn(total_timesteps=1_000_000)
entry.summary: This post details how to get the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and other off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms to work on massively parallel simulators (e.g., Isaac Sim with thousands of robots simulated in parallel) for locomotion tasks. In addition to tuning SAC for speed, the post also explores why SAC fails where PPO succeeds, highlighting a common problem in task design that many codebases share.

entry.title: Two Fragments, or Silence
entry.content:
A personal agent already holds notes one person chose to keep, including early memories they chose to share. The usual action with that store is retrieval plus generation. Return whatever sits near the sentence being written, or produce a paragraph when asked. The open question is narrower. When may the agent interrupt, and how little may it hand back?

The claim is one decision policy. It is not a new theory of analogy, and it is not a measured insight. The default is silence. The only other action returns two original fragments and one gap or causal constraint already written in those texts. The person still restructures the problem. Whether an interruption is worth making is left open. A feeling of insight is not evidence that it was.

The case below is an illustration of that rule, not a result.

One meeting, two fragments

Someone keeps notes on a recurring planning meeting and confirms two fragments. They name the clusters.

Overrun. “The afternoon planning meeting usually runs past four, but the notes say it ended at half past three.” What is missing: who held the previous item open.

Headcount. “The reimbursement count is short the people who stayed after an item was held open.” What is missing: the attendance list for the people who stayed.

On Tuesday they only rewrite the agenda. “Someone keeps holding the previous item open, so I am moving the vote up.” That page meets the overrun note and not the headcount note. The agent stays silent. It does not call a model. A search for notes that mention the meeting would have returned both fragments. This rule does not.

On Thursday they write: “I cannot tell whether we ran long because the same people stayed, and I still do not have the attendance list for those who stayed after an item was held open.” Both missing-pieces meet this sentence, and the person is treating the clusters as separate matters. Only then may the agent sample.

A passing card has four cells. The Thursday sentence. The overrun note, unchanged. The headcount note, unchanged. One line already in the stored text: the headcount note’s “people who stayed after an item was held open.” There is no summary. A sample that only repeats the Thursday sentence, or that adds an instruction to merge the two projects, is dropped with the rest of its set, including the fluent sentence.

Later, the person may change the cut in their own words: these are not two projects until the list exists, so the next step is to get the list. Recognizing the notes, or finding the card clever, does not count. If they cannot say that without reading the card back, it does not count either. Still later, the list may show that staying late and the short count were the same fact, or it may show they were not. That third record is separate. The card made a candidate traceable. It did not make the link true.

The agent already remembers

The agent runs for one person. It reads memories that person chose to place there. It does not read weights or hidden states, and it does not compose a childhood the person never told.

A fragment that can be returned is an unfinished observation, a fact that does not fit, or two accounts that obstruct each other. Each one is stored with its source and with a failure index: what is absent, or what situation would make it relevant again. In the meeting notes, “who held the previous item open” and “the attendance list for the people who stayed” are those indices. A topic word or a mood is not one. A conclusion can point at a fragment. It is not the material.

The index is the opportunistic-assimilation claim. At an impasse, a person stores what is missing, and a later feature of the situation retrieves that unsolved problem. Retrieval is not the new cut . Unsolved problems are remembered better when they are uncommon. A store that marks everything as stuck has thrown the index away .

Clusters are names the person assigns to matters they are still treating as separate. A model that first partitions the store will call neighbors a pair of clusters, and the far question never gets asked. That question is whether two clusters lie under one constraint once “they are two problems” is set down.

The wide constraint is what an impasse hides, so it is not filled in while stuck. On matchstick arithmetic, a constraint of wider scope was harder to release, and transfer followed the type of constraint rather than the surface of the puzzle . The policy borrows the question, not a solver and not the solution rate. While a path still meets its own criterion, as on Tuesday, the agent does not open a change of representation. Progress monitoring, a second account of impasse, supports that restraint and leaves the more general mechanism open .

Nearness is the cheap stage

Documented tools return neighbors during writing , a far prompt at query time , or a clocked highlight, synthesis, or answer . None of those interfaces states the rule above. That is not a finding that they could not.

Analogy maps relations rather than object attributes . A cheap content vector recalls surface neighbors, and structural alignment comes after . A remote story can sit unused until a specific cue. In lab meetings the distant analogies often explained a point to other people and were later forgotten . A shared relation is not the same thing as surface similarity . Far relations on public texts are already returned while a person is generating . What is missing is the decision to stay silent on Tuesday. Spending the model call on the nearest note repeats the cheap stage.

Fluent models largely recognize near narrative analogies. GPT-4 scored below chance on far ones in a zero-shot setting . Two real quotations do not make the proposed relation true.

Silence is the default

Before any generative call, current work is compared only with confirmed failure indices. One cluster, or a gray zone where no pair is clearly nearer than the rest, is silence and zero model calls. Two different clusters, both matching and both nearer than the rest, may be sampled. That comparison is the only gate a first instrument runs.

A violated constraint and a causal mediator are checked only after the gate, by pointing into stored sentences, not by embeddings. Personal stake may bring two clusters up. “Both sides are like this” does not pass. These three are part of the policy and are not claimed as tested. A sample that invents a bridge word, disagrees on the relation, or swaps an endpoint is dropped with its set .

The rule is conservative because the costs are unequal. A false delivery can be taken up as the person’s own judgment. A missed link can return. It does not estimate what an interruption is worth. A fixation is easier to leave after a delay than by pressing on, once a misleading cue has been planted . The agent cannot forget on the person’s behalf. During continuous work it does not light the same cluster again. Setting a problem aside sometimes helps, and the mechanism is not one thing . An empty cycle writes no paragraph. Asking for an insight now is not a collision . Nothing is read from weights, a hidden state, or a prepared-mind signal .

What a delivery is allowed to contain

A pass is traceable. It is not proof.

Stage Question If not
Context Do two clusters’ failure indices meet this work, outside either cluster? Silence
Retrieve Are both endpoints stored fragments with source text? Discard
Relation Is one gap, dropped constraint, or in-text causal link named? Discard
Deliver Is the message only those texts plus that item, tied to this work? Silence
Later Did the cut or the next step change, and can the person restate it? Not a success

At delivery the log records only whether the person recognizes the two fragments. If they do not, the delivery failed. Later, three outcomes stay apart. The cut or the next step changed. The person can restate the link without repeating the card. Subsequent work supports the link. The first two can hold for a false story. In the meeting notes, fetching the list is a changed next step. Whether staying late and the short count were one cause is the third record.

Aha is not evidence

On magic problems, 417 of 1,124 incorrect solutions scored above the mean aha of the correct ones . A locally coherent attempt can miss the real problem space . Fluency and a nod are not the later questions.

Where the memories live

Where the store lives is a separate hypothesis. It does not decide whether the rule helps.

Childhood memories the person chose to share, and personal stakes, are not entries in a company memory other people can read. Mixing them into a shared store threatens privacy and control. It does not, by itself, show that silence would then stop helping. A private store on infrastructure a company pays for does not, by itself, show that the policy helps.

Deleting a fragment removes the edges and undelivered candidates that depend only on it. There is no view onto another person’s graph. After the person has chosen a next step, the only message that may cross to a work agent is a task constraint they release in their own words. Fragments, early memories, stakes, and failure indices stay behind. The work agent does not run this policy.

What would show the policy is idle

No result in this post is an insight measured on a person. The meeting notes illustrate the rule. A log of silence is not a measurement of insight. The instrument is one person, real work, and cases, not puzzle solution rates. Log silence with no generative call, discards with reasons, and deliveries of two originals plus one gap or constraint. The first gate uses only failure indices. The other triggers stay untested. The person answers the later questions.

Baselines are a neighbor list, a request to generate an insight now, and a review clock.

A closed loop with one user, who also wrote the rule, only calibrates the instrument. It checks that the gate stays silent, that the logs are complete, and that entry is cheap enough to continue. It does not falsify the claim that a four-cell delivery changes the cut more often than those baselines. Restructuring happens once, so the same materials cannot take more than one strategy. The comparisons that could falsify the policy assign one strategy to each pair of problems, and the scorer does not know which strategy the pair received.

The following observations, on that later comparison, would falsify the proposal in this form.

  • Recognized neighbor reminders match typed deliveries on a later change in the cut or the next step. The extra constraint check is then idle.
  • The person usually cannot restate the link without repeating the card. The format has closed the restructuring.
  • Prompts during within-cluster work, where this policy stays silent, produce as many later changes. The gate should not be kept .
  • Stake alone, with no named gap, dropped constraint, or causal link in the texts, meets the later criteria. The recall-only rule is then too strong.
  • A bridge word in neither text works as well as a relation already written in both. The check has collapsed into the far-analogy failure already measured .
  • The two later questions hold while subsequent work fails to support the link. Traceability was mistaken for truth.
  • Aha, fluency, or a nod predicts those questions better than the three-material check .
  • Unreleased childhood or stakes are readable by others. The governance hypothesis is then too strong. That result does not refute the intervention rule.

Many days with nothing delivered, when the reasons match the materials, do not falsify the policy. Dozens of deliveries in a day show that the gate failed open. That stops the calibration. It is not yet the comparison above. The decision left open is when returning two fragments and one constraint is worth the interruption.
entry.summary: A personal agent that already holds memories a person chose to share should default to silence. The only other action returns two original fragments and one gap or causal constraint already written in those texts. Semantic nearness is not a trigger, a feeling of insight is not evidence, and whether an interruption is worth making is left open.

entry.title: Wrong Clips, Right Categories: What Cross-Modal Alignment Actually Learns

link.title: Wrong Clips, Right Categories: What Cross-Modal Alignment Actually Learns

entry.content:
Multimodal embedding models map audio and video into a shared vector space, which makes it tempting to train a classifier on sound and run it directly on silent video. Out of the box, that fails badly. On the Audio-Visual Event (AVE) benchmark , a linear classifier trained on Omni Mini 2.3B audio embeddings reaches 95.0% accuracy on audio, but drops to 36.7% balanced accuracy when evaluated on silent video from the same 28 events.

Fitting a single orthogonal rotation between paired training audio and video appears to solve the problem: the exact same audio classifier jumps from 36.7% to 90.5% on silent video. Because an orthogonal transformation only rotates or reflects coordinates without distorting distances inside either modality, it is natural to assume the rotation aligned the two modalities clip for clip.

Then we ran a control that was supposed to break it. Before fitting the rotation, we scrambled the training pairs within each event category, giving almost every guitar soundtrack the wrong guitar video and every helicopter sound the wrong helicopter clip: wrong clips, right categories. We refit the rotation on those mismatched pairs, and accuracy barely moved: 90.1%.

Breaking Audio-Video Pairs Without Losing Accuracy

Imagine two different acoustic-guitar performances. If we swap their soundtracks, the recordings no longer match: the strumming pattern in the audio belongs to a different musician than the hands on screen. Yet for a 28-way event classifier, both clips still carry the same label (Acoustic guitar).

That distinction turns out to be critical for understanding what post-hoc alignment actually learns. In our setup, both the pretrained encoders and the audio classifier stay frozen. We train a multinomial logistic classifier ($C=1$) once on training audio across all 28 AVE categories, and report balanced accuracy (mean per-category recall across the 402 official test clips) so frequent events do not dominate the score. To bridge the two modalities at test time, we fit an orthogonal Procrustes rotation on training audio and video vectors.

To see what signal the rotation actually relies on, we change how the 3,731 training audio and video vectors are paired before fitting it:

  1. Exact clip pairs: Each audio track is paired with its true synchronized video.
  2. Shuffle within event: Every Acoustic guitar audio clip is randomly paired with a different Acoustic guitar video (and likewise within each of the other 27 categories), breaking over 99% of true recording pairs while keeping the event categories matched.
  3. Shuffle all events: Audio and video clips are paired at random across the entire dataset.
  4. Event means only: Individual clips are discarded when fitting the rotation, leaving only the 28 category centroids.

On Omni Mini 2.3B, shuffling pairs within each category yields 90.1% balanced accuracy across three random permutations, nearly identical to the 90.5% obtained from true synchronized pairs. Only when we shuffle across all event categories does accuracy collapse to 4.6%.

We see the same behavior when transferring in the opposite direction (a video-trained classifier evaluated on audio) and on a second model family, Jina v5 Omni-small. On Jina, fitting the rotation on pairs shuffled within each event (88.8%) slightly beats fitting it on the exact clip pairs (88.0%).

Random permutations within a category still leave a few original pairs intact by chance (27 to 35 of the 3,731 training rows in our three Omni seeds). To rule out any contribution from individual clip pairing, we can look directly at the matrix that Procrustes decomposes.

Why Category Averages Drive the Rotation

Orthogonal Procrustes finds the rotation $R$ that best aligns training audio embeddings $A$ with video embeddings $V$ by computing the singular value decomposition of their cross-product matrix, $A^T V$.

If we group the training clips by event category, each embedding vector can be written as its category average (the mean Helicopter vector, the mean Acoustic guitar vector, and so on) plus an instance-specific residual for that particular recording. Because the residuals within each category sum to zero, $A^T V$ splits cleanly into two additive matrices:

Category-centroid alignment

Matches each event's average audio vector to its average video vector. Shuffling clips within a category leaves this matrix untouched.

+
Instance-level residual pairing

Matches clip-specific deviations around each category mean. Shuffling clips within a category scrambles this term.

Instead of scrambling the residual term with a random permutation, we can drop it completely and fit the rotation using only the 28 category averages.

When we do that, Omni Mini 2.3B reaches 90.6% and Jina v5 Omni-small reaches 88.7%. In both models, 28 category centroids alone slightly outperform the rotation fitted on all 3,731 synchronized clip pairs (90.5% on Omni and 88.0% on Jina). When the downstream task is category recognition, instance-level pairing variations act mostly as noise; aligning the category centroids does all the work.

See the exact matrix decomposition Let $A,V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ denote the row-normalized training embeddings. For category $c$ with $n_c$ training rows, write its column-vector means as $\mu_{a,c}$ and $\mu_{v,c}$, and the centered residual rows as $\widetilde A_c$ and $\widetilde V_c$. Because the columns of $\widetilde A_c$ and $\widetilde V_c$ sum to zero, the cross terms between means and residuals vanish: $$ A^T V = \underbrace{\sum_c n_c\mu_{a,c}\mu_{v,c}^T}_{\text{category centroids}} + \underbrace{\sum_c\widetilde A_c^T\widetilde V_c}_{\text{instance residuals}}. $$ The orthogonal transformation minimizing $\lVert AR-V\rVert_F$ is $R=UW^T$, where $A^T V=U\Sigma W^T$ is the singular value decomposition. Fitting on event means replaces $A^T V$ with the first sum and applies the same SVD rule.

Holding Out Categories Breaks the Rotation

When we first saw an orthogonal rotation lift accuracy from 36.7% to 90.5%, we expected it to act like a global coordinate calibration between the audio and video spaces. If the rotation were truly recovering a shared cross-modal reference frame, fitting it on most of the event categories should also help on categories that were held out when fitting the rotation.

To test that hypothesis, we kept the audio classifier trained on all 28 categories so it can still predict every event label. We only restricted the rotation: we fitted Procrustes on paired clips from 21 categories and evaluated how well the rotated classifier recognized silent videos from the 7 categories excluded from the rotation (repeating across four disjoint folds so every category is held out once).

Our global-calibration hypothesis failed in every fold. Across the four fits on Omni Mini 2.3B, the rotation reaches 90.7% on held-out test clips from the 21 categories it saw during fitting, but drops to 24.1% on the 7 categories it never saw. That is 12.5 percentage points worse than using no rotation at all (36.7%). The same pattern holds across all four folds on both models and in both transfer directions.

This drop cannot be explained by having fewer training pairs. Fitting an Omni rotation on a random subset of just 256 true pairs spanning all categories still reaches 79.7%, whereas the category-held-out rotations fail despite using roughly 2,800 training pairs.

Why does holding out categories actively hurt them? Our centroid decomposition points directly to the geometric bottleneck. In a 1,024- or 2,048-dimensional embedding space, 21 category averages span a subspace of rank at most 21, leaving roughly 99% of the dimensions unconstrained by category means. Along the directions spanned by the 21 seen categories, Procrustes aligns audio and video cleanly; along the remaining directions needed to distinguish the 7 held-out categories, the rotation is governed only by residual noise and ends up rotating unseen events into the decision regions of the seen ones. Across the four model and direction settings, 89% to 97% of all errors on excluded categories happen because the classifier mislabels them as one of the 21 categories the rotation saw during fitting (for instance, turning Acoustic guitar videos into Ukulele or Mandolin, and Helicopter videos into Fixed-wing aircraft).

Takeaways for Evaluating Multimodal Alignment

What we found most intriguing in these experiments is not that linear alignment bridges the gap between audio and video embeddings, but how little clip-level correspondence it needs to produce a dramatic accuracy gain. Even though Orthogonal Procrustes never sees explicit class labels during fitting, paired clips from a 28-way benchmark naturally group clips by event. When we evaluate the aligned space with a 28-way classifier, category-level agreement is all the metric rewards, and 28 category averages are enough to match or beat 3,731 exact clip pairs.

That distinction is worth keeping in mind whenever we evaluate cross-modal alignment or representation stitching :

  • When your target task is closed-set recognition over known classes, aligning category centroids (or fitting a rotation on coarsely matched pairs from those classes) is remarkably effective and needs very little data.
  • When you want to claim that an alignment method recovers a generalizable coordinate map, high accuracy on held-out clips from seen categories is not enough.

Two simple controls help separate those two claims: shuffle training pairs within each category to check whether instance-level matching is actually contributing to your score, and hold out categories when fitting the alignment (while keeping them in the classifier) to test whether the transformation generalizes beyond the classes it saw.

Scope and open questions Our experiments evaluate 28-way event classification on the official source-disjoint AVE split across two pretrained checkpoints (`MBZUAI/Omni-Embed-Mini-2.3B` at 2,048D and `jinaai/jina-embeddings-v5-omni-small` at 1,024D), using L2-normalized embeddings, a fixed multinomial logistic classifier ($C=1$), and uncentered orthogonal Procrustes. Fine-grained instance retrieval, regularized or low-rank alignment objectives, and cross-model canonicalization setups may rely on instance correspondence differently and can be audited with the same two controls.
entry.summary: Rotating audio and video embeddings into alignment boosts cross-modal event recognition from 36.7% to 90.5%. Yet shuffling almost every audio-video pair within its category gives nearly the same score (90.1%), while holding out categories breaks transfer completely.
